Addax nasomaculatus, the critically endangered white antelope of the Sahara, exhibits a suite of life-history traits finely tuned to the extreme aridity of its desert habitat. Field studies conducted across the Tenere and ergs of Niger and Chad indicate that after a gestation period averaging 282 days [tg = 282 days] under typical body temperatures of 38 °C [T = 38 °C], female addax give birth to a single precocial calf. Neonatal female calves have a wet weight at birth of approximately 6,000 grams [Wwb = approximately 6,000 grams], representing a substantial initial investment for the mother and endowing the newborn with robust body reserves essential for enduring the sparse and unpredictable forage availability that defines the species' range. This substantial birth mass is an adaptation that allows the calf to follow the maternal herd within days of parturition, minimizing vulnerability to predation during the vulnerable early neonatal stage when concealment is impractical on the open dune fields and gravel plains the addax inhabits.

The developmental trajectory of addax calves unfolds against a backdrop of extreme daily temperature oscillations. Under the average core body temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C] that characterizes the species' stable homeothermy, nutritional independence is achieved when weaning occurs at approximately 198 days after birth [tx = approximately 198 days after birth]. This relatively extended period of maternal milk dependency reflects the low protein content of the desert browse that comprises the adult diet, necessitating a prolonged phase of high-quality nutrition for the growing juvenile before it can efficiently digest the coarse, fibrous vegetation. During this nursing stage, the calf gains mass rapidly on the rich milk provided by the lactating female, who must simultaneously maintain her own body condition through efficient browsing on the scattered Panicum turgidum and Aristida pungens grasses that form the dietary staple across their remaining Saharan strongholds.

Age at sexual maturation in the addax is markedly dimorphic, a pattern common among large desert ungulates where males must compete for breeding access. Females attain puberty at about 2.5 years from birth [tp = about 2.5 years from birth], a timing that allows them to channel resources into completing skeletal growth before the substantial energetic demands of gestation and lactation at a temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C] begin. Males, in contrast, reach puberty earlier, approximately 2 years following birth [tp = approximately 2 years following birth] at a temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C]. This earlier onset of gametogenesis in males, measured under the 38 °C [T = 38 °C] core temperature of the species, does not translate into immediate breeding success; young males must reach a sufficient body size and dominance rank before they can effectively defend a harem of females against older, more experienced rivals, a social constraint that effectively delays their first reproductive opportunity well beyond the point of physiological capability.

Adult body mass exhibits strong dimorphism: females reach approximately 85,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 85,000 grams], whereas adult males, at about 120,000 grams [Wwi = about 120,000 grams], are nearly 40% heavier, a disparity that arises from intense male-male competition for breeding access. This larger body size in males, among the greatest for any antelope in the hyperarid Sahara, reflects both the selection pressure for success in ritualized neck-wrestling bouts and the thermal inertia advantages of a large mass in an environment of extreme diurnal temperature swings. Females, lighter and more mobile, are better able to move across shifting sand seas in search of forage while meeting the energetic costs of pregnancy and lactation.

The species' maximum recorded reproductive rate is constrained by the slow pace of life characteristic of large desert mammals. Females typically produce a single calf once per year [Ri = single calf once per year] at an annual frequency of one reproductive event per year [F_R_i = one reproductive event per year], a schedule that reflects the prolonged gestation and substantial maternal investment. Maximum longevity in the wild is notable for such a challenging environment; reliable field records based on tooth wear patterns and horn annuli indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 28 years [am = approximately 28 years] at 38 °C [T = 38 °C] under the species' typical thermal regime. This extended lifespan, comparable to that of other large African antelopes such as oryx and roan, allows addax to weather the extreme climatic fluctuations of the Sahel and Sahara, maintaining reproductive output across many years despite periodic droughts that can decimate populations and depress calf survival for extended periods.
